description: Byzantine splinter empire on the Black Sea coast (1204–1461) founded by Alexios Komnenos with Georgian support; surviving through commercial utility, controlling the Pontic trade routes and silver mines, and strategic marriages, it outlasted the restored Byzantine Empire by eight years before Mehmed II's naval expedition ended the last Komnenian dynasty.

lifecycle_phases.description: Alexios I Komnenos, grandson of the deposed Byzantine Emperor Andronikos I, establishes the Empire of Trebizond on the Black Sea coast of Anatolia days before or after the Latin sack of Constantinople (1204). The empire controls the crucial Black Sea trade routes between the Silk Road terminus points at Tabriz and the markets of Constantinople. Trebizond's fine harbor, defensible cliffs, and silk/spice trade make it prosperous.

Trebizond survives by skillful diplomacy, marrying its daughters to Ilkhanid Mongol princes, Ottoman sultans, and Georgian kings while maintaining Byzantine cultural prestige. The Komnenos dynasty's claim to be the true Byzantine Empire fades after Michael Palaiologos restores Constantinople (1261), but the commercial city thrives. Trebizond finally falls to Mehmed II's Ottoman navy after a month-long siege (1461).

rise_factors.description: Trebizond controlled the Black Sea terminus of the Silk Road from Tabriz; Genoese and Venetian merchants paid heavily for access to its port, making the empire wealthy far beyond its military power

Trebizond sits on cliffs above a sheltered harbor with the Pontic Alps immediately behind; the city's natural defenses allowed it to withstand numerous sieges while the mountains protected the hinterland from easy overland attack

Trebizond controlled the Black Sea terminus of the Central Asian silk route; merchants from Tabriz, Samarkand, and China passed through the city, generating customs revenues that sustained the empire despite its small territorial base

The Komnenian dynasty's claim to be the legitimate heirs of Byzantium attracted Greek-speaking refugees and ecclesiastical support; Trapezuntine emperors styled themselves "Emperor of the Romans" to claim Orthodox primacy

The Pontic Alps provided natural defensive depth; Trebizond's coastal plain was narrow and the mountain passes were easily blocked, allowing the small empire to survive Turkish and Mongol pressures that destroyed larger neighbors

Trebizond was the Black Sea terminus of the Central Asian Silk Road, receiving Mongol-era caravans carrying silk, spices, and precious stones from China and Persia and taxing the transit trade through its customs house.

decline_factors.description: Mehmed II's Ottoman navy blockaded Trebizond by sea while land forces besieged from the mountains; the 1461 campaign specifically targeted Trebizond as the last Byzantine successor state and the city's commercial wealth made it a priority target

By the 1450s Ottoman control of the Bosphorus and Black Sea approaches cut Trebizond's maritime trade; the city's wealth dried up as merchants shifted to Ottoman-controlled routes, leaving the empire without revenue to pay mercenaries

After the Mongol conquest of Persia, Trebizond paid tribute to the Ilkhanate; though this bought protection, the tribute payments drained reserves and the diplomatic gifts required at court consumed what commercial revenues remained

Mehmed II besieged Trebizond in 1461 with an overwhelming force; Emperor David Komnenos surrendered without battle after the city was isolated, ending the last fragment of Byzantine imperial succession.
